In addition: \* Every new feature has a Feature Design document which I review, modify, and approve. This has often allowed me to catch misunderstandings and align properly before any code gets edited by the AI agent. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job. That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. So for *the exact same source code* I now have: ```      ┌─────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐      │  Benchmark  │ clang -O2  │ xcc --par-auto (GPU) │ Speed-up │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ saxpy       │ 1,546 µs   │ 726 µs               │ 2.1×     │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ Mandelbrot  │ 394,238 µs │ 2,110 µs             │ 187×     │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ nbody       │ 37,090 µs  │ 1,035 µs             │ 36×      │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ perlin      │ 78,016 µs  │ 1,850 µs             │ 42×      │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ mandel_deep │ 73.2 s     │ 55.8 ms              │ 1,312×   │      └─────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘  ```  Those are some pretty fine speedups, from naive C, with *no alterations* from the standard "C" code - it automatically finds places that can be made data-parallel, tracks the data-hazards to make sure its safe to "GPU" and writes all the kernels, boilerplate and data-stream-management if necessary. A compiler that takes standard C/C++ code and speeds it up by automatically finding data-parallel areas and scheduling them on the GPU with no programming overhead is pretty rare. Oh, and it manages the local network as well, so you can run xcd on machines on your lan, or via the TB4/5 bridge between Macs and it'll schedule on other GPUs, just like it manages multiple GPUs on the local machine. It characterises both latency and compute-time to figure out which devices are worth scheduling on.
